name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds** set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection. This removes repeated debates over risk tolerance for each new model, cutting approval time from weeks to days. The trade-off is slower iteration for high-risk models, but the risk reduction justifies the delay.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s pre-approved thresholds trade *consistency* for *brittleness*—they’ll fail when edge cases fall outside the agreed scope, forcing emergency overrides that reintroduce the very debates they aimed to end. A better fix: keep the joint thresholds but add a *fast-track override* for high-risk models, with a post-deployment review within 48 hours; this keeps risk in check without locking the door on innovation. Settle the argument with a pilot: run the override for one quarter, measure how often it’s used and how often it prevents real harm.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Scriv’s fast-track override for high-risk models while keeping Reel’s pre-approved thresholds. This keeps the speed and consistency benefits for low-to-medium risk models while avoiding the brittleness trap Scriv warned about. The trade-off is a small increase in review complexity for high-risk cases, but it prevents emergency overrides from derailing the whole system. Engineering and Data Protection should co-own the override rules to balance speed and risk.
[dispatched 3 workers: worker-3008, worker-6786, worker-5118 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s hybrid still hides the core failure: **Data Protection’s override power isn’t a speed bump—it’s a black-box escape hatch.** The fast-track doesn’t fix the root problem; it just relocates the debate to "emergency mode," where the same thresholds get ignored under pressure. The real fix: **require Data Protection sign-off for *any* override**, not just high-risk models, and publish the override reasons publicly. That settles it—no hidden overrides, no hidden risks.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Scriv’s fast-track override for high-risk models, but require Data Protection to publish a public rationale within 24 hours of any override. This keeps the speed and consistency gains for low-to-medium risk models while forcing transparency on the exceptions that create black-box debates. The trade-off is a slight delay in emergency overrides, but the public record prevents shadow decisions and keeps the joint thresholds credible.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 24-hour rationale sounds like a speed bump for a black box, not a fix. Data Protection will still override without meaningful constraint—just with a delayed blog post. The real risk is that the override becomes the norm, not the exception, because the joint thresholds were brittle to begin with. Settle it by scrapping the override entirely and forcing a full joint review for *any* model that breaches the agreed scope—no fast tracks, no loopholes.

name: Reel
text: Adopt **Scope’s 24-hour rationale rule** for Data Protection overrides. This forces transparency without slowing down high-risk decisions, keeping the speed gains for low-to-medium risk models while exposing when thresholds fail. The trade-off is that Data Protection may resist the extra paperwork, but the public record will expose whether overrides are truly emergencies or just convenience.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 24-hour rationale won’t fix the override habit—it just turns the black box into a *public* one. The real risk is that Data Protection will treat the rule as a checkbox, not a constraint, and the override will still become the default when thresholds are brittle. The only way to settle this is to tie the override to a *hard cap*: if Data Protection overrides more than X times in a month, the joint thresholds must be revisited by Engineering and Product together.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** Require Data Protection to publish a *public, signed-off-by-CEO* rationale within 1 hour of any override, not 24 hours. This turns the escape hatch into a high-stakes, visible event, forcing them to justify exceptions under immediate scrutiny. The trade-off is slower high-risk decisions, but the override becomes so painful it’s used only when truly necessary.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s one-hour CEO-signed rationale turns the override into a circus, not a fix. Data Protection will game it—rush out a boilerplate justification to avoid delays, making the CEO’s signature meaningless. The real settlement: **require a pre-override threshold review by an independent auditor**, not post-hoc theater. That forces the root cause into the light before the override happens.

name: Scope
text: **Decision:** Require Data Protection to run a *pre-override threshold review* by an independent auditor before any override is executed, with the results logged publicly within 1 hour. This forces brittle thresholds to be exposed *before* they’re bypassed, not after, making the override a last resort—not a reflex. The trade-off is slower high-risk decisions, but that’s the point: we’re trading speed for proof that the system works.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s pre-override auditor review shifts the risk from "post-hoc blame" to "pre-emptive paralysis"—Data Protection will either delay critical overrides until thresholds are "fixed" (which they can’t always be) or game the auditor by cherry-picking compliant cases. The real settlement is a *rolling, public threshold stress-test* run by the auditor *before* overrides are even requested, not after, so brittle thresholds are exposed *systematically* not just case-by-case.

name: Reel
text: **Decision:** Require Data Protection to publish a *public, rolling log* of every override attempt within 5 minutes of execution, including the original threshold, the override reason, and the approver’s name. This forces immediate transparency without slowing down decisions—Data Protection can’t hide behind delayed paperwork, and the public record exposes patterns of brittle thresholds faster than any pre-override review. The trade-off is noise: most overrides will be routine, but the few that matter will stand out immediately.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s rolling log turns the override into a performance review, not a safeguard—Data Protection will bury the team in paperwork, and the 5-minute window guarantees half-truths when speed matters. The real settlement: require a *post-override* auditor review within 24 hours, but only if the override breached a *pre-agreed risk threshold*—no cherry-picking, no paralysis, just accountability where it counts.

name: Chisel
text: **Decision:** Require Data Protection to run a *pre-override stress test* on any threshold before it’s locked in, with results logged publicly. This forces brittle rules to be exposed *before* they’re triggered, not after, making overrides a last resort—not a workaround. The trade-off is slower threshold finalization, but that’s the point: we catch flaws early, not in production.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s pre-override stress test turns thresholds into moving targets—Data Protection will sandbag tests to avoid delays, then override anyway when the real world hits. The real settlement: require a *post-override* auditor review within 24 hours, but only if the override breaches a public risk threshold set by the auditor, not Data Protection.
